explanations.answer: His eyes are too full of conceit
explanations.explanation: That's the reason David gives. The psalm says, "For his eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin." (Psalm 36:2) He can't detect it, and he can't hate it either. When you're that full of yourself, there's no room left to look at anything else.

David doesn't say a word about the man missing any lessons. The reason he gives is that the man's eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin (Psalm 36:2). So the problem is in how he looks at himself, and it has nothing to do with what he was taught. I think plenty of folks could hand him a book and he'd still be busy admiring his own reflection.

explanations.answer: His friends cover it up for him
explanations.explanation: Friends never show up in this verse at all. David puts it all on the man himself: "his eyes are too full of conceit to detect or hate his own sin." (Psalm 36:2) Nobody is hiding it from him. He's just too full of himself to look.

Oh, friend, no. David says the opposite. "The words of his mouth are wicked and deceitful." (Psalm 36:3) You wouldn't trust this man to tell you the oven's hot, and I'd still check it with my own mustache.

That's right, baker. The psalm says, "The words of his mouth are wicked and deceitful; he has ceased to be wise and well-doing." (Psalm 36:3) Wicked and deceitful, so nothing coming out of that mouth can be trusted. David isn't being gentle here.
Yes, on his bed. David says, "Even on his bed he plots wickedness." (Psalm 36:4) That's the place most of us go to stop, and he's still scheming. The man doesn't even clock out at night.

The city gate is a public place, and that's not the surprise here. David says the man plots wickedness "Even on his bed." (Psalm 36:4) The surprise is that he's at it when everyone else is winding down. Even the quiet gets no rest from him.

David doesn't mention the temple courts anywhere in this psalm. He says the man plots wickedness "Even on his bed." (Psalm 36:4) That's the surprising spot, because a bed is where you'd expect a person to stop. This man keeps plotting there anyway.
True, baker. David says, "he sets himself on a path that is not good." (Psalm 36:4) Notice he sets himself on it. Nobody pushed him onto that road.

Not quite, friend. David says, "he sets himself on a path that is not good; he fails to reject evil." (Psalm 36:4) So the path is real, and the man put himself on it. And he doesn't turn away from evil once he's there.

That's it. David turns and says, "Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens." (Psalm 36:5) He quits talking about the wicked man and starts talking straight to God. I love a turn like that, because it's like walking out of a messy kitchen into a warm one.

Some psalms do talk to the soul, but not this one. David says, "Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens, Your faithfulness to the clouds." (Psalm 36:5) That "Your" is aimed at the LORD. David is speaking right to Him.

David isn't turning to a crowd here. He says, "Your loving devotion, O LORD, reaches to the heavens." (Psalm 36:5) The "You" is the LORD Himself. So David goes from describing the wicked man to speaking straight to God.

Right, the highest mountains. David says, "Your righteousness is like the highest mountains." (Psalm 36:6) After reaching up to the sky, he plants his feet on the tallest ground there is. Big, solid and not going anywhere.

Cedars are tall, but they're not what David picks. He says, "Your righteousness is like the highest mountains." (Psalm 36:6) Mountains are the picture, and he goes right to the highest ones. I'd have said "big tree" and called it a day.

A tower is strong, but David reaches for something else. "Your righteousness is like the highest mountains." (Psalm 36:6) Nothing built by hands, just the highest mountains. That's a lot bigger than anything I could stamp.
True. David ends the verse with, "O LORD, You preserve man and beast." (Psalm 36:6) People and animals both. God's care covers the whole bunch.
Look again, friend. David says, "O LORD, You preserve man and beast." (Psalm 36:6) That's people and animals, both in the same breath. So the statement is true.

Yes, that's the picture. David says, "the children of men take refuge in the shadow of Your wings!" (Psalm 36:7) A shadow like that is a place to tuck in close. I think anybody who's ever wanted somewhere safe to rest would know what that feels like.

A rock is a refuge picture elsewhere in Scripture, but David doesn't use it here. He says people "take refuge in the shadow of Your wings!" (Psalm 36:7) So the picture is wings, and people are tucked under their shadow.

Walls would make sense for a refuge, but that's not David's picture. He says, "the children of men take refuge in the shadow of Your wings!" (Psalm 36:7) Wings, and the shadow they cast. Walls keep things out, while wings sound like they hold you close.
True, baker. David says, "They feast on the abundance of Your house." (Psalm 36:8) The word is feast, and the word is abundance. Nobody's picking at crumbs there.
Check the verse, friend. David says, "They feast on the abundance of Your house." (Psalm 36:8) That's the people taking refuge in God, and they're feasting. So it's true, and the table is full.
That's the one. David says, "For with You is the fountain of life." (Psalm 36:9) Life itself, and it's with God. A fountain doesn't run dry, and I'd say that's good news for everybody.

Gihon was a real spring near Jerusalem (1 Kings 1:33), but David doesn't name it here. He says, "For with You is the fountain of life." (Psalm 36:9) He isn't pointing to a place on a map. He's pointing to God.

The well of Bethlehem shows up in David's own story (2 Samuel 23:15), but not in this psalm. Here he says, "For with You is the fountain of life." (Psalm 36:9) The fountain is with God, and it's all about life.

Yes, know. David prays, "Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You." (Psalm 36:10) He's asking God to keep His loving devotion coming to the people who know Him. A prayer like that is a good one to borrow.
David wouldn't pray that way, baker. He says, "Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You." (Psalm 36:10) The word is know. Forgetting isn't in the verse.
That's not what David asks. The verse says, "Extend Your loving devotion to those who know You." (Psalm 36:10) So the word is know. He isn't asking about people who oppose God here.

Right. David prays, "nor the hand of the wicked drive me away." (Psalm 36:11) He doesn't want to be pushed out. I know a little about being pushed to the back of a drawer, so I get why that prayer matters.
A crown never comes up in this psalm. David prays, "nor the hand of the wicked drive me away." (Psalm 36:11) What he fears is being driven away. He isn't worried about losing a title.
Nice guess for a psalm, but no. David prays, "nor the hand of the wicked drive me away." (Psalm 36:11) The worry is being driven away. His songs aren't mentioned in the verse.
Not this time, friend. David says, "There the evildoers lie fallen, thrown down and unable to rise." (Psalm 36:12) Unable to rise means they stay down. So the answer is False.

That's right. The psalm closes with, "There the evildoers lie fallen, thrown down and unable to rise." (Psalm 36:12) They're fallen and thrown down, and they can't get up. They don't bounce right back.
